history.t: Iraq invades Kuwait: Brent spot from $15 in early July to $41 in late September.
Asian crisis and an OPEC output rise: Brent near $10.
The all-time nominal high: Brent spot $143.95 on 3 July 2008, then the financial crisis.
OPEC decides not to cut against US shale: prices halve into 2016.
Covid: with Cushing filling up, WTI spot closes at −$36.98 a barrel (the May future at −$37.63).
Russia invades Ukraine (24 Feb 2022); Brent spot reaches $133 on 8 March.
War with Iran; traffic through the Strait of Hormuz collapses.

events.t: US–Israeli strikes on Iran; the Revolutionary Guard declares the Strait of Hormuz closed.
IEA members agree the largest stock release ever, 400 million barrels (426 pledged by 19 March).
Physical Brent at an all-time high ($144.68 Dated, Argus); a ceasefire that evening, futures fall $20 the next day.
US naval blockade of Iranian ports begins.
The UAE leaves OPEC and OPEC+.
Islamabad Memorandum signed; both blockades lifted; Ras Tanura loads again from 29 June.
The memorandum collapses after attacks on ships; the US blockade returns on 14 July; Houthi blockade of the Red Sea from 20 July.
Drones shut the Saudi East–West pipeline; Yanbu loadings stop until a partial restart on 22 September.
US retail diesel record, $6.529 a gallon (EIA weekly).
G7 agrees to release up to 100 million barrels, diesel first; EIA Brent spot $135.51.

gapEvents.t: Cushing glut: the Permian and Bakken boom fills the Oklahoma hub before pipelines to the Gulf exist; Brent spot trades up to $29.59 over WTI (23 Sep 2011).
The US lifts its 40-year ban on crude exports.
WTI Midland enters the Dated Brent basket (cargoes from June 2023).
Record tanker rates: the futures gap reaches about $13.80.

usEvents.t: Horizontal drilling and fracking spread from gas to oil (Bakken, then Eagle Ford and the Permian).
Covid: negative WTI; output falls by about 2 mb/d within weeks.

hormuz.title: Before the war
hormuz.text: About 80 ships a day; some 20 mb/d of crude and products through the strait, a fifth of world consumption. Gulf exports by all routes about 24 mb/d.

hormuz.title: The strait closes
hormuz.text: Strikes on Iran on 28 February; the Revolutionary Guard closes the strait. Gulf producers shut in more than 10 mb/d within two weeks. Saudi Arabia pushes crude west through the East–West line to Yanbu, the UAE fills its line to Fujairah.

hormuz.title: Bypasses at full stretch
hormuz.text: Bypass exports reach 7.8 mb/d, total Gulf exports 10.5 mb/d, 14 mb/d below February. A ceasefire on 7 April crashes futures by $20; the US blockades Iranian ports from 13 April.

hormuz.title: The memorandum
hormuz.text: The Islamabad Memorandum is signed on 17 June and both blockades are lifted; Ras Tanura loads again from 29 June. Gulf exports climb to 16.1 mb/d.

hormuz.title: Blockades again
hormuz.text: The memorandum collapses on 7–8 July; the US blockade returns on 14 July and the Houthis declare a blockade of the Red Sea. Hormuz carries 7.6 mb/d; Gulf exports by all routes fall to about 13 mb/d.

hormuz.title: Dark transits
hormuz.text: Drones shut the East–West line on 11 September. In October PortWatch counts about four transits a day, yet Kpler sees 11.6 mb/d leave through the strait: most tankers sail with their transponders off, and non-Iranian Middle East exports are back at their pre-war level.
